::: {.team-note}
## Summary {.unlisted}

This page covers five feasibility conditions that must be in place before committing to a randomised controlled trial (RCT), five randomisation designs and when to use each, and the most common problems that arise after the lottery.
:::

By this point you have mapped your intervention's causal logic, defined what you want to find out, and chosen the indicators you will use to measure it. The question this step answers is whether you can actually run a randomised evaluation to get those answers - and if so, how to design it.

An RCT is not always possible. Before investing time and resources in a randomised design, a managing authority needs to check whether the basic conditions are in place. Once they are, the choice of randomisation method matters: different intervention shapes call for different designs. This page covers both.

***

## Five conditions for a feasible RCT

Work through these five questions before committing to a randomised design. If the answer to the first three is not yes, an RCT is unlikely to be feasible and you should explore alternative approaches with your evaluation team.

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
### 1. Is the intervention oversubscribed? {.unlisted}
An RCT requires more eligible applicants than available funding slots. If you can support everyone who qualifies, there is no basis for a lottery - and no credible comparison group. Oversubscription is the single most important precondition.
:::
::: {.card-e}
### 2. Is there enough time? {.unlisted}
Randomisation must happen before the first grant is awarded. If the intervention has already launched, it is too late. Planning must ideally begin at the intervention design stage.
:::
::: {.card-e}
### 3. Is there a legal basis? {.unlisted}
Most national frameworks were designed around ranking or first-come-first-served selection and say nothing about random assignment. Explicit permission - either in existing regulations or through an intervention-specific instrument - must be confirmed before proceeding.
:::
::: {.card-e}
### 4. Is there political and institutional buy-in? {.unlisted}
An RCT requires sustained commitment from the managing authority and any intermediate bodies involved in delivery. If key stakeholders are not on board, or if political changes could interrupt the evaluation midway, the investment may not be recoverable.
:::
::: {.card-e}
### 5. Can the outcomes actually be measured? {.unlisted}
The indicators selected in [Step 3](02.04-indicators.qmd) must be observable - through administrative records, a survey, or both. If the primary outcome cannot be reliably measured for both treatment and comparison groups, the evaluation will not produce credible results even if the design is sound.
:::
:::

::: {.soft-panel}
**Is randomisation permitted under your national legal framework?**

Before designing the lottery or scoring mechanism, confirm that your national legal framework - and the specific legislation governing your intervention - either explicitly permits randomisation as a selection method or is flexible enough to accommodate it.

Most national frameworks were designed around ranking or first-come-first-served selection and say nothing about random assignment. A clear legal basis is the precondition for experimental evaluation to happen at all. [See the legal framework page](02.04b-legal.qmd) for country examples, key legal elements, and practical steps.
:::


## Randomisation must be designed in from the start

The most common mistake is treating randomisation as something that can be added once the intervention is already running. It cannot. By the time the first grant is awarded, the comparison group must already be defined, the eligibility rules must be locked in, and the baseline data should have been collected. 

:::: {.example .romania data-map="romania-ne"}
[North&#8209;East Romania: building the eligibility pool]{.tag}
```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div>Outreach<br><span style="font-weight:400;color:#6B6455">Social media, radio, and events in 20+ cities</span></div>
  <div>Online applications<br><span style="font-weight:400;color:#6B6455">About one hour to complete</span></div>
  <div>Automatic screening<br><span style="font-weight:400;color:#6B6455">Stops as soon as a criterion fails</span></div>
  <div style="background:#F2C94C;border-color:#F2C94C">1,038 eligible MSMEs<br><span style="font-weight:400">Screened from over 1,500 applicants by September 2023</span></div>
</div>
```
North-East Romania combined three steps that are usually separate - application, eligibility check, and baseline data collection - into a single online survey. This meant that by the time the eligibility pool was confirmed, the baseline data was already in hand. In October 2023, 519 of the 1,038 eligible firms were randomly selected to receive a grant. The other 519 became the comparison group.
::::

## Do you have enough units?

To detect the impact of an intervention, you need enough units in both the treatment and comparison groups. Too few units and even a real effect may be invisible - ordinary variation between units drowns out the signal. The technical term for this is statistical power, but the practical question is simple: is your eligible pool large enough?

The answer depends on how large an effect you expect, how much units vary on the outcome of interest, and how confident you want to be in the result. An evaluator will run a power calculation to translate these inputs into a minimum required sample. [More details on power calculations](02.04a-power.qmd)

Lessons learned from projects within the EuroCOMP Lab inform about potential ways for reaching large enough numbers.

:::: {.myths-grid}

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>Invest heavily in outreach - especially to reach new beneficiaries</summary>

Standard outreach channels - newsletters, social media posts, agency websites - consistently fail to reach the firms that EU interventions are designed to serve. Firms without prior experience of EU funding, smaller firms, and firms in rural or remote areas are systematically less likely to apply, not because they are ineligible but because they do not know the intervention exists or lack the resources to navigate the application process.

Effective outreach requires direct, personalised engagement: in-person events, road trips to municipalities, collaboration with mayors and local business associations, and hands-on application support. Experimenting with different outreach approaches - and measuring which ones work - can significantly expand the eligible pool and improve the quality of applications.


::: {.example .romania data-map="romania-ne"}
[North&#8209;East Romania]{.tag}

In North-East Romania, the World Bank randomised outreach activities across 46 cities, selecting 26 for road-trips where a consultant explained the call and helped firms complete the pre-assessment survey. Cities that received road-trips produced 110 applications compared to 71 in cities that did not - a 55% increase. Applications from road-trip cities also came from significantly smaller firms (12.6 employees on average, compared to 19.6 in comparison cities). Compared to previous calls, the total number of applicants tripled and the number of eligible firms more than doubled. This small experiment demonstrated both the effectiveness of in-person mobilisation and the value of embedding experimentation into intervention implementation.
::::

</details>


<details class="myth-box">
<summary>Eligibility criteria should remain broad enough</summary>

On one hand, eligibility criteria should not be too restrictive to target a large enough number of firms. On the other hand, eligibility criteria should remain specific enough to identify firms with the highest potential to benefit. Eligibility criteria should be linked to the intervention's Theory of Change to avoid that wrong firms enter the pool.

::: {.example .case data-map="romania-sm"}
[Romania (South-Muntenia)]{.tag}

In South-Muntenia (Romania), the World Bank found that eligibility criteria for an innovation support intervention were quite restrictive, taking into account the firm landscape in this region. The World Bank worked with the managing authority to adjust the criteria to target a higher number of firms.
::::

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>Base intervention design on evidence of need</summary>

Interventions that are designed without a prior assessment of beneficiary needs frequently suffer from misalignment: either too few firms apply (under-subscription), or the intervention attracts firms that are not its intended target. Both problems are expensive - leading to repeated calls, unused funds, or support that reaches firms that would have done well without it.

A baseline needs assessment - conducted before the intervention launches - allows the managing authority to understand the regional landscape, calibrate grant sizes and eligibility thresholds, and anticipate demand more accurately. Where uncertainty about demand remains, piloting different intervention elements before full-scale rollout can reduce the risk of costly mismatches.

::: {.example .case data-map="italy"}
[Italy]{.tag}

In Italy, a minibond intervention pre-identified 289 eligible firms, of which only 30 applied - a hit rate of 10.3%. Of the 19 firms that ultimately issued a minibond, most had access to alternative financing and may not have needed the intervention at all. A prior needs assessment could have revealed that the intervention's terms were less attractive than alternative instruments already available in the region - including zero-interest loans and non-repayable grants from earlier interventions - and that the design needed to be adjusted accordingly before launch.
::::

</details>


<details class="myth-box">
<summary>Simplify the application process</summary>

Complex, document-heavy application processes disproportionately burden firms that are least familiar with EU funding - the very firms that interventions are often designed to reach. When compliance requirements are similar regardless of grant size, small firms face the same administrative burden as large ones, often pushing them to hire consultants and creating a market for intermediaries that adds cost without adding value.

Application requirements should be proportionate to the amount of funding requested. Processes should be fully digital, integrated with existing administrative databases wherever possible, and capable of providing real-time eligibility feedback so that firms can assess their likelihood of success before investing significant time in an application.

::: {.example .romania data-map="romania-ne"}
[North&#8209;East Romania]{.tag}

In Romania, the pre-assessment survey was designed to do three jobs simultaneously: collect baseline data for the evaluation, assess firm eligibility in real time, and provide firms with enough information to decide whether to proceed - all within approximately 40 minutes. Survey responses were automatically cross-referenced with official firm data, enabling instant verification of core eligibility criteria. Firms that did not meet the requirements were informed immediately, saving them from investing further time in a formal application that would have been rejected. Eligible firms received individualised benchmark reports comparing their digitalisation levels to similar firms in their region, providing added value to participants regardless of their eventual selection outcome.
::::

</details>


<details class="myth-box">
<summary>Use the application process to exchange information</summary>

The application process is typically treated as a one-way flow of information: firms submit data to the managing authority. In practice, it can also be a vehicle for delivering useful information and tools to firms - raising awareness about a topic (digitalisation, innovation, energy efficiency), helping firms identify investment needs, and providing benchmarks that inform business decisions regardless of whether the firm is selected for support.

Firms that receive useful information during the application process are more engaged, better prepared to make investment decisions if selected, and more likely to view the experience positively even if they are not funded.

::: {.example .case data-map="croatia"}
[Croatia]{.tag}

In the Scinergy pilot in Croatia, the World Bank supported an extensive outreach and information campaign that included a dedicated project website, a LinkedIn campaign with paid promotions, appearances in television and online media, presentations at industry events and scientific institutions, and webinars targeting thousands of firms. The campaign was structured around a business-science matchmaking concept, providing firms with substantive information about how to collaborate with research institutions - not just how to apply for a grant. The initiative attracted widespread media coverage and generated strong interest in applications well before the call officially opened.
::::

</details>

::::
